1.pericope_label: The order to turn back, and the trap laid for Pharaoh

schools.summary: Calvin works at the etymology of Pi-hahiroth and gives it up honestly, preferring a root that means to engrave, since the rocks there look cut as with a mallet; but he holds the word mouth makes it certain the defile was narrow and rock-walled, with the sea closing the other side, so that Israel had been laid as in a sepulchre. He settles on confounded for their entanglement, since they could find no way out of it. The stratagem he reads as a bait set to catch the tyrant as a fish is hooked: had Israel simply walked out unmolested, the earlier miracles would not have testified their redemption sufficiently, whereas being shut in and seeing nothing before them but death they had to confess themselves saved by God's hand out of the abysses. Gill contributes the topography, citing a traveller on the breach in the range by which one may turn short off into the valley of Baideah and follow it down to the sea.

Henry marks how strange the order was: a stage or two more would have brought them to Horeb, the place appointed for their serving God, and instead they are turned short off away from Canaan towards the sea, where at Etham no water had lain in their path. It was God himself, then, who put them into the straits — which might have assured them that when his purposes were served he would as surely bring them out, since he sometimes raises difficulties in his people's way that he may have the glory of subduing them. He reads the disclosure to Moses as a courtesy: Pharaoh had a design to ruin Israel and God therefore a design to ruin Pharaoh, using the king's own shrewdness against him, for the deeper the entanglement looked the readier he would be to come on; and since all men are made for their Maker's honour, those he is not honoured by he will be honoured upon.

Clarke takes Pi-hahiroth for the mouth or bay of Chiroth, Migdol for the tower, probably a fortress guarding the bay, and Baal-zephon for the lord of the watch, likely a temple with a light kept burning as a mark for shipping. He sets out the position exactly — the sea in front, Pharaoh behind, fortresses to right and left, and not one boat prepared — so that if they were saved at all the arm of the Lord must be seen in it and the Egyptian gods shown to be nothing; and he has God withdraw restraining grace and let the king rush on. Wesley describes them more briefly as shut in by mountains and by deserts.

Ellicott plots the march: it had run almost south-east to the head of the Bitter Lakes, and the command turned them south, keeping them inside Egypt with the Lakes now on their left. He rejects the rendering of the verb as an order to retrace their steps, since the march was to bring them to a sea they had not yet reached, and rejects the Mediterranean, which Exodus never calls simply the sea. All three place-names he holds unidentifiable, small places near the head of the Gulf of Suez, and turns that into evidence: so many obscure names argue a knowledge of Egyptian ground unlikely in any Israelite who had not walked it. The word he renders confused or perplexed, and reads it from Pharaoh's side, who saw them marching south with the desert before them and judged they had lost their way. Keil grants the turn was not out of the way for a passage through the sea, though by human reckoning it was a foolish one; gives the king's thought as a prison whose door is shut; and holds that what turned his heart was not the change of route but the flight itself, which left him time to muster chariots.

5.pericope_label: The report brought to Pharaoh, and the pursuit made ready

schools.summary: Calvin denies that the flight was news at all, since it had been anything but secret; what was reported were the circumstances, and hearing that they fled in haste the king judged the slightest obstacle might hold them. He is hardest on the courtiers, who blame their own inertness as though they had not been ten times overcome — the stupidity of the wicked, who dread only God's present hand and forget everything they have seen. The muster he reads the same way: only the day before the Egyptians were frightened almost to death and crying that all was over, and now they collect an army as though their forces were untouched, which shows with what obstinate audacity the wicked go forward. To the objection that six hundred chariots were no match for six hundred thousand men he answers that they expected an unwarlike crowd with women and children mixed into it, and would not have been disappointed had God not been against them. In Israel's going out with a high hand he hears a reproof: their security had freed them from all care and the desire of calling on God had cooled with it, since safety breeds drowsiness, so that the danger, coming unlooked for, produced the greater fear. Gill takes the chariots for war chariots of iron, perhaps fitted with scythes to cut men down, chosen partly for speed, to overtake a people several marches ahead, and partly for strength; and reads made ready as ordered to be made ready.

Clarke points out that Pharaoh cannot have been ignorant of the departure, having licensed it: fled must mean they had gone for good, which he had not expected, having granted only three days' journey — and what weighed most with an avaricious king was the property carried off and the service lost. He describes the chariot crew as two or four horses and three men aboard, of whom the driver seldom fought, the second shielded him, and the third alone was properly the combatant. Wesley says the king would not own that they went with his consent, being willing to have it represented as a revolt; reads the captains as command distributed among several officers; renders the high hand boldly and resolutely; and thinks the king took no foot at all, his business requiring haste.

Ellicott reckons the cost in economic terms: the emigration left eastern Egypt a solitude, suspended the royal works and threw commerce into disorder, neither king nor people having understood beforehand what the loss of six hundred thousand labourers would mean. He notes that kings of that period almost always led their armies in person, and that made ready means ordered to be made ready. The number he sets against what is known, the largest well-attested muster being under four thousand chariots, so that six hundred chosen ones is credible, most likely a division of the royal guard; all the chariots of Egypt must not be pressed, and the captains were set over the whole force rather than over each. The verb of Israel's going out he would render were going out, and takes the high hand for confidence and boldness, perhaps a touch of pride, as of men who had brought the Egyptians to beg them to leave. The word horsemen he defends against those who make it the riders in the chariots, since it is the one Hebrew word with that sense and there is abundant testimony that Egypt used cavalry, whatever the sculptures show; the army that follows he takes for the infantry, so that the host had all three arms. Keil closes with the sight that met Israel, the Egyptian army advancing, and their great alarm.

10.pericope_label: Israel’s fear at the sea, and the answer of Moses

schools.summary: Calvin adds that the suddenness made the fright worse, no messenger having gone before. He refuses the division of the people into those who prayed and those who murmured, since the two statements stand together in one sentence and cannot be referred to different persons: on his reading the cry came neither from faith nor from ordered affection but was forced out by a confused impulse, nature driving all men in trouble to pray without their embracing God's mercy or relying on his power, and the wild cries against Moses are the proof that the calling on God had been thoughtless. The scoff about graves he sharpens: not content with preferring Egyptian graves to the death they feared, they jeer as though Egypt had no room to bury them, forgetting that they had themselves been brought miraculously out of the grave. He doubts the silence of Moses, thinking it improbable that such cries were let pass unrebuked, and conceives that he chastised their insolence but omitted the reproof from his narrative to show that God's kindness outran their impiety; stand still he glosses as keep quiet, no man having occasion to move a finger. Gill takes the middle ground on the murmur, noting that the Targum confines it to the ungodly of that generation while he judges the body of the people meant, and reads the Lord's fighting concretely, by commanding the wind and the waves.

Henry describes the trap — numerous indeed, but all on foot, unarmed, undisciplined and dispirited by long servitude, with impassable rocks on one hand, forts on the other, the sea in front and the Egyptians behind, so that no way lay open but upwards, and thence their deliverance came. He separates two responses: some cried to the Lord, their fear setting them praying, since God brings us into straits that he may bring us to our knees; others cried out against Moses. In their complaint he finds a sordid contempt of liberty, when it were better to live God's freemen in the open air of a wilderness than the Egyptians' bondmen in the smoke of the brick-kilns, and he counts this the first of the ten provocations for which Israel was sentenced to die in the wilderness. The reply of Moses he admires: he answered not these fools according to their folly, but instead of chiding comforted them, disheartened neither by the threatenings of Egypt nor the tremblings of Israel — for it is our duty, when we cannot get out of our troubles, to get above our fears.

Clarke reports Calmet's version of the division, the pious appealing to God while the irreligious murmured, and observes that had the prayer been joined with faith we should not find them murmuring immediately after. He agrees that no resistance was intended, since of that there was no hope: they were not even to be workers together with God, but to see a deliverance worked without them, and were to have no part in the honour of the day. Wesley stands with Henry throughout, both on the hopelessness of the position and on the restraint of the answer Moses gave.

Ellicott meets the objection that six hundred thousand men had no business fearing Pharaoh's hasty levy: Herodotus puts Egypt's whole armed strength at four hundred and ten thousand and not half of that could have been mustered, but numbers were not the point, since the Egyptians were trained and well-armed and the Israelites were neither — a million Persians having been slaughtered like sheep by forty-seven thousand at Arbela, so the fear was legitimate. The question about graves he makes a bitter jest meaning that they might as well have died in Egypt as here, and calls the reproach unjust, since in the main they had acquiesced in Moses' proceedings and let him act in their name. Keil settles the sense of the closing promise against the Greek: the words are inverted, and mean not that they would see the Egyptians in that manner but that they would never see them again.

15.pericope_label: Go forward: the rod, the hardening, and the pillar moved behind

schools.summary: Gill takes the crying of Moses for mental prayer without voice, which proves that assurance had not made him neglect the means; notes that the rod was the same that had done so many wonders in Egypt; and accepts the Jewish identification of the angel with Michael only if the uncreated Word is meant by it. Calvin rejects the reading that extends God's question to the whole people, whose prayers were not directed to God at all: Moses had prayed apart, and the answer means only, weary yourself with crying no more. He warns that those are rash who promise particular blessings without a special word from God, Moses having proclaimed nothing he had not first heard; and he uses the hardening against the doctrine of bare permission, since the Egyptians would never have dared enter a sea plainly armed against them unless God had blinded them. Of the angel he observes that he who has been called Jehovah throughout the narrative is here called the Angel, and takes him for the only-begotten Son, adding the corollary that the glory which enlightens the faithful darkens unbelievers, so that it is no wonder if the brightness of the Gospel blinds the reprobate still.

Henry takes it that Moses lifted up his heart without speech, and that these silent prayers of faith prevailed more than Israel's loud outcries of fear, the question being no rebuke but a dismissal — why press a petition already granted, with the hosts of Israel to command? He reports a suggestion that Moses had prayed less for the deliverance, of which he was sure, than for the pardon of the murmuring, so that the command to go forward was itself the intimation of pardon; they looked to be turned right or left, and instead are sent straight to the sea-side, as though a fleet of transports lay ready for them. The same power, he notes, could have frozen the waters to pass over, but infinite wisdom chose rather to divide them to pass through, the way of salvation pitched upon being always the most humbling. He weighs the emphatic I three ways — sovereignty, since God's grace is his own; power, since none but the Almighty can make a heart soft and no other can make it hard; and justice, it being righteous to put men under his wrath who have long resisted his grace. The angel he has leave the front, where a guide was no longer wanted, for the rear, where a guard was, lighting Israel through the water and confounding the pursuers, who lost sight of their prey as they were about to lay hands on it — the word and providence of God having a dark side towards sinners and a bright one towards Israelites indeed.

Clarke turns the question to the comfort of the inarticulate: the heart of Moses was deeply engaged though probably not a word was formed, and the language of sighs and tears is as intelligible to God as speech, so that a man who cannot pray may weep, and if tears are denied him may sigh. He observes that neither Moses nor his rod could effect anything in a work belonging to omnipotence alone, but that he had to appear in it so Israel might see whom God had chosen; describes the cloud's two faces, the luminous side lighting the camp all the night of the passage and the dark side denying the Egyptians any benefit of it; and allows that a cloud so appointed might be called a messenger, though he thinks the Angel of the covenant appeared. Wesley stands with Henry on the silent prayer, on the pardon intimated by the command, and on the pillar's removal to the rear.
Keil holds that the words carry no reproof but an admonition to resolute action.

21.pericope_label: The east wind, the sea divided, and the passage by night

schools.summary: Gill notes the rod was in the hand as directed, and that what the poets say of Bacchus, whose rod was lifted upon the rivers, is truer of Moses, whose had been raised over Egypt's rivers and now over the Red Sea. Calvin admires the restraint of the telling, Moses using no ornament of language, the bare recital being the more powerful for it. On the wind he holds both ends at once: God could have dispelled the waters without any motion of air, and raised the wind only to show that all nature obeys him, yet no wind could have dried that sea without the secret power of the Spirit working beyond nature's ordinary course. He agrees the pillar made the passage convenient enough by night, and reckons the time from evening to dawn, since so vast a multitude could not have crossed in an hour; and he ends on the modesty of the narrator, who, told to divide the sea with his uplifted rod, changes the expression when he writes it and says the waters went back at God's command, content with a minister's character and leaving God alone the author.

Henry sets the dividing of the sea among its Scripture parallels, a type of baptism, the passage figuring the conversion of souls and the Egyptians' perdition the ruin of the impenitent. He distinguishes two signs — the instituted sign of the outstretched hand, which showed the thing done in answer to prayer, and the natural sign of a strong east wind, which showed it done by the power of God, whom the winds and seas obey, for the God of nature has not tied himself to nature's laws but dispenses with them when he pleases. He makes the crossing a bay of two or three leagues over, notes that the wall of water is mentioned twice and that the pillar behind kept the Egyptians from charging their flank, and supposes with Wesley that Moses and Aaron ventured first into the untrodden path and Israel followed — a passage that would make the later march through the wilderness seem less formidable, since those who had followed God through the sea need not fear to follow him anywhere. It was night, he adds, and no moonshine night either, being seven days past the full, so the people had no light but the pillar's, the more awful for that, though where God leads us he will light us.

Clarke argues that the east wind cannot have divided the waters at all: at the crossing the sea runs some fourteen fathoms deep, and a wind able to lift that mass out of its bed would have blown six hundred thousand people away with it. He concludes that God parted the waters by sovereign power, and that the east wind, always noted as parching, came afterwards to dry the bed — God honouring nature where it can act and acting alone where it cannot; and on the authority of Bruce he makes the crossing about four leagues, easily done in a night. Wesley stands with Henry on the width of the bay and on the march itself.

Ellicott offers the opposite reconstruction to Clarke's. If the Bitter Lakes were joined to the sea by a narrow shallow channel, a south-east wind driving the lake water north while the ebb tide drew the sea water south would leave a stretch of channel dry until the wind shifted; Scripture says nothing of the tide because there was nothing unusual in it, but an Egyptian tradition has Moses waiting for the ebb, and whether God carried nature further than this he says we are not told. Keil declines to fix the quarter the wind blew from, since Hebrew has words only for the four points and the place of the crossing is unknown, and explains the dividing as a flowing away of the water to north and south, leaving the bed dry in the middle with the heaped water standing as a wall on either side.

22.pericope_label: The wall of waters, the host troubled, and the sea returned

schools.summary: Gill sets out the four watches and puts the morning watch between three and six; collects the guesses about the chariot wheels, the Targum having them cut off, some thinking them broken by hailstones and Jarchi that fire burnt them; and reports from Aben Ezra the opinion that Israel did not cross at all but took a semicircle and came out on the same shore. Calvin reads the Lord's looking as a deliberate opening of the Egyptians' eyes, that too late they might see where their mad impetuosity had brought them and perceive that they contended not with men but with God, and that, struck with that astonishment, they could not make the shore in time. He finds a purpose in the daylight: the waters had been heaped in the night, but it was fitting that the Egyptians should perish by day and the sun make their destruction visible, while God urged on their very flight, as though they drowned themselves on purpose. He has no patience with the historians who explained the whole by the tides of the gulf.

Clarke makes the wall the proof of the miracle: had the crossing been managed by an extraordinary ebb there could have been no waters standing on the right hand and the left, still less standing against every law of fluids while Israel passed and turning obedient to gravity the moment the Egyptians entered; and he thinks it intolerable that men who receive this as revelation should labour to prove it had nothing miraculous in it. He adds Calmet's reckoning of the morning watch at about four, supposes the cloud suddenly took a fiery appearance, or that the Egyptians were appalled by the thunder, lightning and driving rain the psalmist records, tempests enough to terrify the horses and throw the column into confusion, and reports from Josephus fifty thousand horse and two hundred thousand foot, of whom not one was left to carry the news. Wesley says the same of the winds and lightnings in brief, adding terror of mind besides; turns the wheels into a sentence, that they had driven furiously and now drove heavily, their axle-trees failing, having flown on the back of Israel as the hawk upon the dove and now crying out to flee; and buries Pharaoh himself in the deep as a perpetual monument of divine justice.

Ellicott answers Clarke from usage: a wall in Scripture means any protection whatever, and here the waters covered Israel on either flank; the poets heightened it and spoke of waters standing in a heap, but to build on that the claim that the water congealed into a hard substance, as Kalisch does, is to turn poetry into prose. He has the morning watch between two and six, times the order to stretch out the hand as soon as Israel was across, and describes the end — the white-crested waves advancing on both sides, the chariot wheels clogged, men and horses weighed down with armour, and the flood upon them while they were still far from shore. Whether Pharaoh himself drowned he treats as an open question to be settled by general considerations rather than by this verse: only the chariots and cavalry entered the sea, so the king might have stayed with the reserve; had he been killed the silence of Scripture and of the Egyptian annals would be strange; and Menephthah, to whom the indications point, reigned at least eight years and once declined to lead his army against a Libyan invasion, pleading that the god forbade him to leave Memphis. Keil explains the return mechanically: the east wind having ceased, the water flowed together from north and south, and a west wind drove the waves into the faces of the fleeing Egyptians.

30.pericope_label: Israel saw the Egyptians dead, and feared the LORD

schools.summary: Gill dates the salvation precisely: though it was six or seven days since they had departed, they could not properly be said to be saved until this day, when all the enemies that pursued them were destroyed, and this was the twenty-first of the month, the seventh and last day of the passover, a holy convocation to the Lord. He notes that the word rendered work is properly hand, and that what Israel considered was the power which turned the waters that had divided for their safety back upon their pursuers; and he describes the fear as an awe of God's greatness upon their minds and a sense of his goodness upon their hearts, working a filial and godly fear, with belief that he is faithful to his word, able to do all things, and wise to do them in the fittest season. Calvin finds the same double aspect in the spectacle, there being no difficulty in distinguishing wrath from fatherly love where an unwarlike multitude was so miraculously preserved and an army formidable on every account destroyed in the depths. He takes fear here for the reverence that kept them in the way of duty, since they were not merely struck with dread but drawn to devote themselves to a goodness they had so sweetly experienced, and reads believed as added expositively, marking the principal part of that reverence. The affection he grants was general, the recognition of God's hand bowing them to obedience, but he holds the ardour soon passed from the greater number, who are moved only by what is visible and present, while some seed remained in a few; and from the joining of Moses with the Lord he draws the rule that those who faithfully deliver God's commands are to be attended to as if he had openly descended from heaven.

Clarke draws a practical inference from the bodies on the shore: by the extraordinary agitation of the waters multitudes were cast up, and from their spoils Israel was probably furnished with riches, and especially with clothing and arms, essential afterwards in the wars with the Amalekites, Basanites and Amorites — if they did not get their arms this way, we do not know how they got them, since there is no reason to believe they brought any out of Egypt. On the closing verse he has them convinced that God's power was unlimited both in judgment and in mercy, and satisfied that not one thing had failed of all the good spoken concerning them. Wesley reads the bodies as studied contempt: the Egyptians were very curious in preserving the bodies of their great men, and here the grandees of Egypt lie heaps upon heaps, as dung upon the face of the earth. Of the fear he says they were now ashamed of their distrusts, and in the mind they were then in would never again despair nor talk of returning to Egypt — adding how well it were for us if we were always in as good a frame as we are sometimes.

Ellicott takes the verse as evidence of authorship: on one who saw the sight it would make a great impression, but to later generations it was nothing, since it had no further consequences, so that its being recorded at all indicates the pen of an eyewitness. Keil calls the great work the might Jehovah had displayed upon Egypt, and distinguishes two ends that do not exclude each other: besides the glory gotten upon Pharaoh promised earlier in the chapter, the passage through the sea was designed to establish Israel more firmly in fear and in faith, so that they should discern not only their merciful deliverer but the holy Judge of the ungodly. Faith in the Lord he ties inseparably to faith in Moses as the servant of the Lord, which is why the miracle was wrought through his hand and staff.
